title: Design and Implement AI Guardrails and Controls
intro: Guardrails and the testing that proves they work: input handling, content filtering and context boundary validation around the model; architectural guardrails for autonomous agents through the harness and orchestration patterns; functional, performance and load testing adapted to non-deterministic AI; and stress testing and validation that the system handles exceptions safely.
objectives: Design layered guardrails for inputs, context and outputs, keeping instructions and untrusted content in separate, labelled boundaries
Use the agent harness and orchestration patterns, such as plan-then-execute and privileged and quarantined models, to limit autonomous behaviour
Plan functional, performance and load tests for AI systems using evaluation sets, repeated runs, tail-latency targets and realistic traffic
Apply stress testing and fault injection, and validate that exceptions fail closed, reveal nothing and leave no half-finished actions

sections.title: Guardrails for inputs, outputs and context boundaries

scenes.title: Guardrails around the model
scenes.sub: Input handling, content filtering and context boundaries
scenes.say: A model alone can’t reliably tell instructions from data, or safe content from harmful content. Guardrails are the systems around it that do that work. | This video covers the guardrail architecture for inputs, outputs and context: prompt sanitisation, content filtering, and context boundary validation.

scenes.title: A guardrail pipeline
scenes.say: Here is a typical guardrail pipeline. Input arrives from users, and also from retrieved documents and tool results. | Input guardrails normalise text, run classifiers for injection attempts, jailbreaks and off-topic requests, and redact sensitive data. | Context assembly builds the prompt with clear, labelled boundaries between instructions and untrusted content. | The model, ideally safety-tuned, generates a response. | Output guardrails filter harmful content, check grounding against sources, validate structure, and catch data leaks. | Only then does the result reach the user or a downstream system.

scenes.title: Context boundary validation

items.d: System, user and tool content apart
Delimit and label it as data
No tool calls from documents alone

scenes.say: Context boundary validation keeps instructions and data apart. | Use separate roles for system instructions, user input and tool or retrieved content, rather than pasting everything into one block. | Mark untrusted content clearly, with delimiters and labels that say it is data, not instructions. | Use models trained with an instruction hierarchy, where system and developer instructions outrank user input, which outranks tool content. | Protect the context budget, so safety instructions are never truncated to make room for long documents. | Validate content before it is added to the context. | And limit what untrusted content can trigger: a retrieved document should never cause a tool call on its own.

scenes.title: Kinds of filter
scenes.say: Filters come in three main kinds. | Rules catch known patterns and formats, such as card numbers. Trained classifiers catch harm categories and injection attempts. A large model acting as a judge can catch nuanced breaches of policy. | Rules are fast and predictable. Classifiers are fast with broad coverage. Judges are flexible, and can explain their decisions. | But rules are easy to evade, classifiers produce false positives and drift over time, and judges are slow, costly, and can themselves be manipulated by the content they inspect.

items: Guardrails sit before, around and after the model
Keep instructions and untrusted content in separate, labelled boundaries
Combine rules, classifiers and judges; measure their error rates
No guardrail stops every injection: limit what outputs can do
scenes.say: To recap. | Guardrails sit before, around and after the model. | Keep instructions and untrusted content in separate, labelled boundaries, and protect safeguards from truncation. | Combine rules, classifiers and model-based judges, and measure their false positive and false negative rates. | And remember that no guardrail stops every injection, so limit what outputs and actions can do.

blocks.md:
### Input handling
- **Normalisation:** Unicode normalisation; removing invisible, zero-width and control characters; decoding obfuscation such as encoded text, where appropriate.
- **Validation:** length and token limits, file types and sizes, rate limits (Module 3.6).
- **Classification:** detectors for prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, off-topic or out-of-scope requests, and abusive content. Cloud providers and open-source projects offer such classifiers, including dedicated safety models that label prompts and responses against a policy.
- **Redaction:** detect and mask personal data and secrets before prompts reach external models (Module 3.4).
- **Indirect sources:** apply the same checks to retrieved documents, web pages, emails and tool results, which are the main route for indirect prompt injection.

### Context boundary validation
| Technique | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Role separation** | Uses the API’s distinct system, user and tool roles rather than one concatenated prompt |
| **Delimiting and labelling** | Wraps untrusted content in clear markers and tells the model to treat it as data ("spotlighting"); variants mark every token of untrusted text or encode it |
| **Instruction hierarchy** | Models trained to prioritise system and developer instructions over user input, and user input over tool or retrieved content |
| **Context budgeting** | Reserves space for system instructions and safety text, and truncates untrusted content first |
| **Provenance tags** | Attaches source and trust level to each chunk, so downstream logic and filters can treat content differently |
| **Trigger limits** | Prevents content from low-trust sources from directly causing tool calls or other actions |

These techniques **reduce** injection success; none eliminates it. Assume some injections will succeed, and enforce authorisation and action limits outside the model (Modules 4.1 and 4.6).

### Content filtering
- Define a **content policy**: categories (such as hate, harassment, violence, self-harm, sexual content and dangerous activities), severity levels and actions (block, warn, route to a human).
- Apply filters to **both** inputs and outputs; tune thresholds per use case and audience.
- Combine **rules** (fast, precise for known patterns), **classifiers** (broad and fast) and **LLM judges** (nuanced but slow and themselves vulnerable to injection).
- **Measure** false positive and false negative rates on representative test sets, and monitor them in production; over-blocking drives users to unapproved tools.

### Output handling
Encode for the destination, validate structure against schemas, check grounding and citations, run DLP and moderation, and never execute output directly (Module 3.5). For streaming, buffer or filter chunk by chunk (Module 4.1).

### Guardrail operations
Version guardrail configurations as code, test them in the pipeline (Module 4.3), log decisions for monitoring (with privacy protections), review blocked and allowed samples regularly, and update for new attack techniques found by red teams and threat intelligence.

blocks.title: Guardrail questions
blocks.md: Look for **layered** guardrails on inputs, context and outputs, with **measured** error rates, and for designs that **separate instructions from untrusted content**. Beware answers claiming a single filter or prompt "prevents" prompt injection; the best answers also **limit what a fooled model can do**.

blocks.title: Which guardrail technique is this?
pairs: Retrieved web pages are wrapped in markers and labelled as untrusted data
Spotlighting
The model gives developer instructions priority over text inside a tool result
Instruction hierarchy
Long documents are cut before any safety instructions are
Context budgeting
A classifier flags a prompt as a likely jailbreak attempt
Input classification
A reply containing an unapproved link is held for review
Output guardrail

blocks.title: The disappearing safeguards
blocks.md: A legal research assistant builds each prompt by pasting the retrieved case documents first and its system instructions last, in a single block of text. With long documents, the prompt exceeds the context window and the end is cut off. Testers notice the assistant now answers questions far outside its approved scope.

o: Raise the maximum document length, so that fewer documents are needed for each answer
Use the system role, reserve budget for instructions, and truncate retrieved content first
Ask users to keep their questions short, so that more space is left for the instructions
Repeat the safety instructions several times in the middle of the retrieved documents
q.why: Instructions belong in their own role with protected space, and untrusted content should be what gets truncated. Longer documents make the problem worse, user behaviour isn’t a control, and instructions buried in content are easily lost or overridden.

q.q: A RAG assistant inserts retrieved web pages into its prompt as plain text, directly after the system instructions. Which change BEST strengthens the context boundary?
o: Add a sentence at the end of the prompt asking the model to ignore any instructions it finds
Pass retrieved content in a separate, clearly delimited and labelled section that is treated as data
Increase the context window size so that more web pages fit into the prompt at once
Retrieve web pages only from well-known sites that rank highly in search engine results for the query
q.why: Separating and labelling untrusted content as data, ideally in a distinct role, helps the model and downstream checks treat it differently from instructions. A closing instruction is weak, bigger contexts add attack surface, and search ranking says nothing about safety.

scenes.title: The harness, not the horse
scenes.say: You can’t make a model perfectly obedient, but you control everything around it: the code that runs its loop, executes its tools, and decides what it may do next. | This video covers architectural guardrails for autonomous AI: the agent harness, orchestration patterns, and the limits that keep agents safe.

scenes.title: What the agent harness controls

layers.label: Allowed actions
layers.sub: Which tools exist, with which scopes

layers.label: Checks on every step
layers.sub: Validate arguments and policy before execution

layers.label: Human checkpoints
layers.sub: Approval for high-impact or irreversible steps

layers.label: Budgets
layers.sub: Steps, time, tokens, cost and tool calls

scenes.say: The agent harness is the code that runs the agent loop. It, not the model, is where safety is enforced. | It defines which actions exist at all: which tools the agent has, and with which scopes. | It checks every step before execution: are the arguments valid, and does policy allow this action now? | It inserts human checkpoints for high-impact or irreversible steps. | It enforces budgets on steps, time, tokens, cost and tool calls. | And it applies stop conditions: a kill switch, loop detection, and escalation to a person when the agent is stuck or uncertain.

scenes.title: Workflows and open-ended agents
scenes.say: An important design choice is how much freedom to give. | In a workflow, your code fixes the steps in advance, and the model fills in parts. In an open-ended agent, the model decides the steps at run time. | Workflows are highly predictable and easy to test. Open-ended agents are less predictable and much harder to test. | So prefer workflows wherever the task is well understood, and use open-ended agents only where their flexibility is genuinely needed.

scenes.title: Keeping untrusted content away from control
scenes.say: One powerful pattern keeps untrusted content away from the part of the system that decides what to do. A user makes a request. | A planner model turns it into a plan, but never sees untrusted content such as emails or web pages. | A separate, quarantined model reads that untrusted content, for example to summarise an email, and has no ability to call tools. | Its results come back as structured values, validated and treated as data, not instructions. | And the harness calls tools according to the planner’s plan, so instructions hidden in the content have no route to control actions.

scenes.title: Guardrails for agent actions
scenes.say: Six more guardrails shape what agents actually do. | Read before write: start agents with read-only tools, and require more assurance for anything that changes data. | Prefer reversible actions: drafts instead of sends, soft deletes, and dry runs that show what would happen. | Require human approval for irreversible actions, such as payments, deletions and messages to outside parties. | Cap the impact, with limits on amounts, volumes and recipients. | Trace every step: plans, tool calls, results and decisions, for monitoring and investigation. | And make sure agents can be stopped quickly, with kill switches and circuit breakers.

items: The harness, not the model, enforces safety
Prefer workflows; use open-ended agents only where needed
Keep untrusted content away from planning and control
Read-only first, reversible actions, approvals, caps, tracing, stop
scenes.say: To recap. | The harness around the model, not the model itself, is where safety is enforced. | Prefer fixed workflows, and use open-ended agents only where their flexibility is needed. | Keep untrusted content away from the components that plan and control actions. | And start read-only, prefer reversible actions, require approval for irreversible ones, cap impact, trace everything, and be able to stop.

blocks.md:
### The agent harness
The **harness** (also called the scaffold or runtime) is the code that runs an agent: it sends prompts to the model, parses its proposed actions, executes tools, manages memory and state, and decides when to stop. Because the model only *proposes* actions, the harness is the natural enforcement point:
- **Action space:** the tools registered, their scopes and credentials (least privilege; Module 4.6).
- **Pre-execution checks:** schema validation of arguments, policy checks (for example, "refunds only to the customer’s own account, below £200"), and allow-lists for destinations.
- **Human-in-the-loop checkpoints** for high-impact, irreversible or unusual actions, with enough context for a real decision rather than a rubber stamp (Module 2.6).
- **Budgets:** maximum steps, wall-clock time, tokens, cost and tool calls per task; maximum delegation depth for multi-agent systems.
- **Stop conditions:** loop and repetition detection, confidence or error thresholds that trigger escalation, and an external kill switch (Module 5.7).
- **State and memory controls:** what is remembered between sessions, who can write to shared memory, and validation of memory contents (memory can be poisoned).
- **Observability:** structured traces of every plan, call and result.

### Orchestration patterns
| Pattern | Idea | Security benefit |
|---|---|---|
| **Workflow first** | Fixed steps in code; the model fills in parts | Predictable, testable, smaller action space |
| **Plan, then execute** | The plan is produced and checked before any tool runs | Policy can review the whole plan; injected content can’t add steps mid-run |
| **Dual model (privileged and quarantined)** | A planner that never sees untrusted content; a quarantined model that processes content but can’t act | Separates control flow from untrusted data; research systems such as Google DeepMind’s CaMeL (2025) build on this with capability tracking |
| **Supervisor or critic** | A separate component reviews proposed actions | Second check, though a model-based critic can also be fooled |
| **State machine** | Only defined transitions are allowed | Prevents agents jumping to unexpected actions |
| **Least-privilege sub-agents** | Specialised agents with narrow tools | Limits the blast radius of any one compromised agent |

### Design principles
- **Assume the model will sometimes be manipulated** (OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection) and limit the consequences (OWASP LLM06: Excessive Agency).
- **Make the dangerous path hard:** high-impact tools need approval, separate credentials and stricter validation.
- **Fail safe:** on errors, timeouts or uncertainty, stop and escalate rather than retrying indefinitely or guessing (Section 4).
- **Keep humans meaningfully involved:** approvals must show what will happen, why, and with what data, so reviewers can catch problems.

blocks.title: Agent guardrail questions
blocks.md: When asked how to make an agent safer, prefer controls in the **harness**: fewer and narrower tools, policy checks before execution, approvals for irreversible actions, budgets and stop conditions. "Instruct the agent to be careful" is never the best answer.

blocks.title: Name the orchestration pattern
pairs: Fixed steps in code; the model fills in parts
Workflow first
The whole plan is checked before any tool runs
Plan-then-execute
A planner never sees untrusted content; another model reads it but can’t act
Privileged and quarantined models
Only defined transitions between states are allowed
State machine
Specialised agents each get a narrow set of tools
Least-privilege sub-agents

q.q: An email-triage agent reads incoming messages and can forward emails and create calendar invites. Which architecture BEST limits the impact of instructions hidden in incoming emails?
o: A longer system prompt that warns the agent to watch for suspicious emails
A planner that never reads raw emails, a quarantined summariser, and approval for forwards
A second agent that reads every incoming email first and decides whether it looks malicious or safe
Giving the agent access to more tools, so that it can handle more cases itself
q.why: Separating untrusted content from the component that controls actions, and requiring approval for external sends, means hidden instructions can’t steer tool use directly. Prompt warnings and a model-based gatekeeper can both be fooled, and more tools increase the blast radius.

sections.title: Functional, performance and load testing for AI systems

blocks.title: Testing systems that don’t repeat themselves

scenes.title: Testing systems that don’t repeat themselves
scenes.say: Traditional tests expect the same input to give the same output. AI systems give different answers each time, slow down unpredictably under load, and cost money per request. | This video covers functional, performance and load testing adapted for AI systems.

scenes.title: Functional testing for AI

items.d: Blocks bad inputs, allows good ones

scenes.say: Functional testing for AI needs six adaptations. | Build evaluation sets: representative cases with the expected behaviour, including edge cases. | Score with metrics rather than exact matches: accuracy, groundedness, task success. | Run tests many times and measure pass rates, because outputs vary. | Run the full regression suite on every change: model, prompt, retrieval index or guardrail. | Include security behaviour tests: does the system block known-bad inputs and still allow good ones? | And if a model grades the outputs, calibrate it against human judgement first.

scenes.title: Latency is a distribution, not a number
scenes.say: Performance targets must describe the whole distribution. In this illustrative chart, half of requests complete within about one and a half seconds under normal load, but the slowest one per cent take nearly five. | Under peak load, the median barely moves, but the tail explodes: the slowest one per cent take over eleven seconds. | So set targets on high percentiles, such as the ninety-fifth and ninety-ninth, and measure time to first token and throughput as well as total time.

scenes.title: Performance and load tests
rows: Does it hold up at expected volume?
Realistic traffic mix and token sizes
scenes.say: Performance and load testing answer different questions. | Performance testing asks how fast the system is for a single user. Load testing asks whether it holds up at the expected volume. | Performance tests measure latency percentiles and tokens per second. Load tests measure throughput, error rates, queueing and how autoscaling behaves. | And both must use realistic inputs: long prompts and long outputs cost far more than short ones, so a load test with tiny prompts proves very little.

scenes.title: Making tests trustworthy

items.d: Keep test cases out of training

scenes.say: Tests are only useful if they can be trusted. | Don’t use production personal data in test sets; use synthetic or properly masked data. | Version test sets, pinned and protected, with changes reviewed like code. | Guard against contamination: if test cases leak into training data, scores become meaningless. | Agree pass thresholds in advance, and link them to the release gates. | And budget for cost, because running large evaluation suites against large models is expensive.

items: Evaluate with metrics over many runs, not exact matches
Regression-test every change to model, prompt, retrieval or guardrails
Target tail latency, time to first token and throughput
Load-test with realistic traffic and token sizes
scenes.say: To recap. | Evaluate AI behaviour with metrics measured over many runs, not exact matches. | Regression-test every change to the model, prompt, retrieval or guardrails. | Set performance targets on tail latency, time to first token and throughput. | And load-test with realistic traffic and realistic token sizes.

blocks.md:
### Functional testing
| Practice | Details |
|---|---|
| **Evaluation sets** | Curated inputs with expected behaviour or reference answers, covering typical cases, edge cases, multilingual inputs and known failure modes; versioned and access-controlled |
| **Metrics** | Task-specific: accuracy and F1 for classification; groundedness, citation accuracy and answer relevance for RAG; task completion and tool-call correctness for agents |
| **Non-determinism** | Run each case several times; use pass-rate thresholds; fix temperature or seeds where the platform allows, while also testing production settings |
| **Regression** | Any change to the model version, prompts, retrieval index, embedding model, tools or guardrails triggers the suite (Module 4.3) |
| **LLM-as-judge** | Model-based grading scales evaluation; calibrate it against human ratings, keep the judge model pinned, and watch for bias towards longer or more confident answers |
| **Security behaviour** | Guardrail tests with known-bad prompts (from red teaming and public jailbreak and injection datasets) and known-good prompts, reporting both false negatives and false positives |
| **Fairness and safety** | Disaggregated metrics by group, and safety benchmark suites relevant to the use case (Module 3.5) |

### Performance testing
- **Latency:** time to first token (what users feel), total response time, and percentiles (p50, p95, p99), because tail latency drives user experience and timeouts.
- **Throughput:** requests and tokens per second per instance, and how it changes with batch size and context length.
- **Cost per request**, especially for long contexts and multi-step agents.
- **Guardrail overhead:** measure each check’s added latency (Module 4.1).

### Load testing
- Model **realistic traffic**: the mix of request types, prompt and output lengths, concurrency, and daily or seasonal peaks.
- Observe **queueing, autoscaling, rate limiting and quota behaviour**, GPU memory pressure (key-value caches grow with context length), and error rates.
- Include **dependencies**: model provider rate limits, vector databases, tool APIs.
- Run against **production-like environments**, with care for cost and provider limits; coordinate with hosted providers before large tests.
- Compare results to **SLOs** and capacity plans (Module 4.2).

### Trustworthy test data
Use synthetic or masked data rather than production personal data; protect and version test sets; keep evaluation data out of training to avoid **contamination** (Module 1.3); and record test results as evidence for release gates (Module 4.3).

blocks.title: Testing questions
blocks.md: For AI, good answers mention **evaluation sets and metrics** rather than exact-match tests, **repeated runs** for non-determinism, **regression on every change**, and **realistic load** including long prompts. Testing guardrails means measuring **both** missed attacks and wrongly blocked legitimate requests.

blocks.title: Testing vocabulary
cards: Versioned test inputs with expected behaviour or reference answers, covering typical and edge cases.
The share of repeated runs that meet the criteria, used because outputs vary.
The response time that 95% of requests beat; the slowest 5% take longer.
The wait before a streamed answer starts to appear, which is what users feel.
Test cases leaking into training data, which makes scores meaningless.

q.q: A team swaps its chatbot to a newer model version that scores higher on public benchmarks. What should happen before the change reaches users?
o: Nothing further, because the new version scores higher on public benchmarks
Run the system’s own regression, safety and guardrail suites against the new version
Ask a few colleagues to chat with it for an hour and report any problems they notice
Deploy it to everyone, and roll back if the number of complaints increases
q.why: Public benchmarks don’t measure your prompts, data, guardrails or use case. The system’s own regression, safety and guardrail tests, with agreed thresholds, show whether the new version is fit. Informal chats and complaint-driven rollback leave users to find the problems.

sections.title: Stress testing and exception handling validation

scenes.title: Break it before attackers do
scenes.sub: Stress testing and exception handling validation
scenes.say: Systems rarely fail under normal conditions. They fail at the edges: under extreme load, with malformed input, when a dependency goes quiet, or when the model says something unexpected. | This video covers stress testing and validating that an AI system handles exceptions safely.

scenes.title: Kinds of stress test

items.d: Sustained load for hours or days

scenes.say: Stress tests push the system beyond normal conditions. | Spike tests send sudden surges of traffic. | Soak tests apply sustained load for hours or days, revealing memory leaks and slow degradation. | Breakpoint tests increase load until something fails, so you know where the limit is and how failure looks. | Input extremes: very long, malformed or unusual inputs, such as strange encodings or empty fields. | Dependency failures: slow, erroring or missing services. | And agent edge cases: loops, tool errors, and tasks with no valid path forward.

scenes.title: Injecting failures on purpose
scenes.say: Chaos engineering applies the scientific method to failure. Start with a hypothesis: for example, if the moderation service fails, replies are held rather than sent unchecked. | Inject a fault deliberately: make the model slow, return rate-limit errors, or take the vector database offline. | Observe what actually happens: system behaviour, logs, alerts, and what users see. | Compare the result with the hypothesis. | Fix anything that didn’t behave as expected, and add the scenario to the regular test suite. | And repeat, through scheduled game days and automated tests in the pipeline.

scenes.title: What safe exception handling looks like

items.d: Security checks never skipped on error
No stack traces or system prompts
Roll back or flag partial work

scenes.say: Exception handling validation checks six behaviours. | The system fails closed: an error in a security check never means the check is skipped. | Errors reveal nothing useful to an attacker: no stack traces, internal addresses or system prompts in messages. | Retries use backoff and limits, then stop and escalate, rather than looping forever. | Bad model output is handled: invalid structured output, unexpected refusals and nonsense are caught, not passed on. | Partial work is rolled back or clearly flagged, so an agent never leaves half-finished actions behind. | And every exception is logged and, where it matters, alerts the operators.

items: Spike, soak, breakpoint, input-extreme, dependency and agent tests
Inject faults deliberately and compare against a hypothesis
Fail closed, reveal nothing, retry with limits, handle bad output
Roll back partial work; log and alert on exceptions
scenes.say: To recap. | Use spike, soak, breakpoint, input-extreme, dependency and agent edge-case tests. | Inject faults deliberately, and compare the result against a stated hypothesis. | Make sure the system fails closed, reveals nothing in errors, retries within limits, and handles bad model output. | And roll back partial work, while logging and alerting on every exception that matters.

blocks.md:
### Stress testing
| Test | Purpose | AI-specific angle |
|---|---|---|
| **Spike** | Behaviour under sudden surges | Autoscaling lag for GPU capacity, which can take minutes; provider rate limits |
| **Soak (endurance)** | Behaviour over long periods | Memory growth in inference servers and caches; slow drift in agent memory |
| **Breakpoint** | Where and how the system fails | Whether it degrades gracefully (Module 3.6) or collapses |
| **Input extremes** | Robustness to unusual inputs | Maximum-length prompts, huge files, malformed encodings, many attachments, deeply nested structures |
| **Dependency failure** | Resilience to outages and slowdowns | Model API timeouts and HTTP 429 rate-limit responses, vector database outages, tool failures |
| **Agent edge cases** | Safe behaviour when tasks go wrong | Tool errors, contradictory results, impossible goals, loops, exhausted budgets |

**Chaos engineering** makes failure testing systematic: state a hypothesis about steady-state behaviour, inject a fault in a controlled way (starting in test environments, with a limited blast radius), observe, and fix gaps. **Game days** rehearse failures with the operations team, including AI-specific runbooks (Domain 5).

### Exception handling validation
Write explicit test cases for each failure mode, each with the expected safe behaviour:
- **Fail closed** for security functions: if moderation, DLP or authorisation is unavailable, hold or refuse rather than proceed (Module 3.6).
- **Safe error messages:** no stack traces, file paths, internal hostnames, system prompts or configuration in user-facing errors; detailed diagnostics go to logs only. Error messages are a common source of system prompt and infrastructure leakage.
- **Bounded retries** with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, and escalation after a limit.
- **Robust parsing of model output:** validate structured output against schemas; handle refusals, truncation at token limits, and hallucinated tool names or arguments; never pass malformed output downstream.
- **Transactional behaviour for agents:** compensate or roll back partial actions, or flag them clearly for human follow-up; make actions idempotent where possible, so retries don’t duplicate payments or messages.
- **Timeouts everywhere**, including on tool calls and agent runs.
- **Observability:** log exceptions with correlation IDs, alert on unusual error rates, and include them in post-incident reviews.

### Fuzzing
Fuzz inputs, prompts and tool outputs with random and structured variations to find crashes, parsing errors and unsafe behaviours. LLM-generated test inputs can widen coverage, and adversarial variants overlap with AI red teaming (Module 6.4).

### Making it routine
Put stress and failure tests in the pipeline where practical, run larger exercises before major releases and on a schedule, and track findings to closure. Each incident and red-team finding should add a regression test.

blocks.title: Exception handling questions
blocks.md: The safest behaviour under failure is usually **fail closed, reveal nothing, stop and escalate**. Watch for distractors that keep the service running by **skipping a security check**, show **detailed errors** to users, or **retry indefinitely**.

blocks.title: Which test would find this?
pairs: Memory use on inference servers creeps up over three days
Soak test
A product launch triples traffic within five minutes
Spike test
Load is raised step by step until requests start failing
Breakpoint test
A prompt full of broken encoding crashes the request parser
Input-extreme test (fuzzing)
The vector database is switched off during a test window
Dependency failure test (chaos engineering)

blocks.title: The retry storm
blocks.md: During a traffic spike, a model provider starts returning HTTP 429 rate-limit errors. Every client of an internal AI service retries each failed request immediately, and the platform also retries on the clients’ behalf. Traffic to the provider multiplies, the rate limiting lasts far longer than the spike, and users see failures for an hour.

o: Retry immediately but from more servers, so that the backlog clears faster
Exponential backoff with jitter, retry limits, one retry layer and a circuit breaker
Remove rate limits from the provider contract, so 429 errors can never occur
Show users the provider’s raw error message so that they know to wait
q.why: Backoff with jitter spreads retries out, limits and a single retry layer stop amplification, and a circuit breaker pauses calls to a struggling dependency. Faster retries make the storm worse, and the other options don’t fix the behaviour.

q.q: During a failure test, the vector database behind a support assistant is taken offline. The assistant keeps answering, inventing policy details, and shows users an error containing the database’s internal hostname. What should be fixed?
o: Nothing, because the assistant stayed available throughout the test
Fail safely without retrieval, and return a generic error with details logged internally
Show the full error to users so that they can report the problem to support
Add a second vector database in another region, so that this test can no longer cause any failures
q.why: Without retrieval the assistant should decline or degrade to a safe mode, not invent answers, and user-facing errors should reveal nothing internal while diagnostics go to logs. Availability with wrong answers isn’t success, and redundancy alone doesn’t fix unsafe failure behaviour.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN purpose of context boundary validation?
o: To make sure the prompt fits inside the model’s maximum context window
To keep instructions apart from untrusted content, and check what enters the context
To compress retrieved documents so that more of them fit into each prompt sent to the model
To translate every input into English before it reaches the model
quiz.why: Boundary validation separates and labels trusted instructions and untrusted data, and checks content before it is added, which reduces indirect injection.

quiz.q: Why should safety instructions be protected when context budgets are tight?
o: Longer system prompts always produce more accurate and better-grounded answers from the model
If they are truncated to make room for documents, the safeguards silently disappear
Providers charge less for system instructions than for user content
Safety instructions are needed to authenticate the user to the model
quiz.why: Context budgeting should truncate untrusted content first, so that system and safety instructions are never cut to fit long inputs.

quiz.q: What is a key weakness of using an LLM as a content-filter judge?
o: It can only detect patterns such as card numbers and phone numbers
It is slower and costlier, and can be manipulated by the content it inspects
It can’t explain why it reached any of its decisions
It must be retrained from scratch every time the organisation’s content policy changes
quiz.why: Model-based judges are flexible but slow and expensive, and because they read the content, injected instructions can sway them.

quiz.q: In an agent system, where is safety MOST reliably enforced?
o: In the model’s system prompt, which tells it what it must never do
In the harness, which checks and executes every proposed action
In the user interface, which hides dangerous options from users
In the model’s training data, which teaches it good behaviour
quiz.why: The model only proposes actions; the harness decides what runs. Policy checks, approvals, budgets and stop conditions there don’t depend on the model obeying.

quiz.q: Why should a well-understood task use a fixed workflow rather than an open-ended agent?
o: Workflows always produce more creative and varied results for users
Fixed steps are predictable and testable, with a smaller action space
Open-ended agents can’t call tools or use retrieval at all
Workflows remove the need for any input or output guardrails
quiz.why: Fixing the steps in code limits what can happen and makes behaviour testable. Open-ended agents add flexibility, and risk, that a known task doesn’t need.

quiz.q: In the privileged and quarantined model pattern, what can the quarantined model do?
o: Plan the whole task, and then call any of the tools that the plan requires
Read untrusted content and return structured results, but not call tools
Approve high-impact actions on behalf of the human reviewer
Rewrite the system prompt when the user’s request changes
quiz.why: The quarantined model processes untrusted content without any ability to act, so instructions hidden in that content can’t reach the tools.

quiz.q: Why should AI functional tests report pass rates over repeated runs?
o: Repeated runs are needed to warm up the model’s cache before testing
Outputs vary between runs, so a single pass or fail can mislead
Regulators require every test case to be run at least ten times
Repeating tests reduces the cost of each individual evaluation
quiz.why: Non-determinism means the same input can pass once and fail the next time. Pass rates over many runs give a reliable picture.

quiz.q: Which performance measure BEST reflects how responsive a streaming chatbot feels to users?
o: The total number of GPUs available to the serving cluster
Time to first token, tracked at the higher percentiles
The average length of the answers the chatbot gives
The number of tokens in the model’s context window
quiz.why: Users feel the wait before text starts to appear, and tail percentiles show the worst experiences that averages hide.

quiz.q: Why does a load test that uses only short prompts prove very little?
o: Short prompts are blocked by most input guardrails
Cost and capacity scale with tokens, so long requests behave very differently
Load tests are only valid when they use real production personal data from customers
Short prompts make autoscaling switch off during the test
quiz.why: Realistic traffic includes long contexts and outputs, which use far more GPU memory and time. Tiny prompts overstate capacity.

quiz.q: What does a soak test MAINLY reveal?
o: How the system copes with a sudden surge of traffic
Problems that only appear over time, such as memory leaks
The exact point at which the system starts to fail as load keeps rising
Whether malformed inputs crash the request parser
quiz.why: Soak tests apply sustained load for hours or days. Spike, breakpoint and input-extreme tests cover the other cases.

quiz.q: What should a user-facing error message from an AI service contain?
o: The full stack trace, so that users can report the fault precisely
A generic message, with detailed diagnostics written only to internal logs
The system prompt, so that users understand why their request failed
The internal hostname of the failing service, to speed up support
quiz.why: Error messages are a common leak of internals and system prompts. Show users a safe, generic message and keep the details in logs.

quiz.q: Why should agent actions be idempotent where possible?
o: Idempotent actions always run faster than other kinds of agent action
Retrying them after an error won’t duplicate payments or messages
Idempotent actions don’t need any human approval
They let agents skip the harness’s policy checks safely
quiz.why: Failures lead to retries. If repeating an action has the same effect as doing it once, retries can’t cause double payments or duplicate sends.

exam.q: A customer-facing assistant’s input classifier blocks 4% of legitimate requests, and staff report that frustrated customers are switching to an unapproved public chatbot. What should the security team do FIRST?
o: Turn the input classifier off until a better product can be procured and tested
Measure false positives on representative data, then tune thresholds and policy per use case
Block access to the public chatbot at the firewall, so customers have no alternative to use
Tell customers in the interface that the blocks are for their own protection and safety
exam.why: Guardrails need measured error rates in both directions. Tuning against representative data reduces over-blocking without removing protection. Switching the filter off drops a control, blocking alternatives ignores the cause, and messaging doesn’t fix the error rate.

exam.q: A RAG assistant summarises supplier documents. A tester shows that a document containing hidden instructions can make the assistant include a phishing link in its answers. Which combination BEST reduces this risk?
o: A stronger system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions it finds in documents
Labelled boundaries for retrieved content, plus output checks such as URL allow-lists
Retrieving fewer documents per question, so that each answer is based on less content
Retraining the embedding model on a larger and more varied set of supplier documents
exam.why: Layered controls work best: delimit and label untrusted content to reduce injection, and validate output, for example by allowing only approved domains, so a successful injection can’t deliver a malicious link.

exam.q: A finance agent can read invoices and issue payments. An injection test makes it pay a fraudulent invoice of £9,800. Which harness control MOST directly prevents a recurrence?
o: Fine-tuning the agent on examples of fraudulent invoices so it learns to spot them
A pre-execution policy check with payment limits, verified payees and human approval
Telling the agent in its system prompt to double-check every invoice before paying it
Moving the agent to a larger model that is more resistant to prompt injection
exam.why: Controls in the harness don’t rely on the model resisting manipulation: payee verification, limits and approval stop a fooled agent from completing the payment. Fine-tuning, prompts and bigger models all still depend on the model.

exam.q: A research agent browses the web and writes reports into a shared drive. During testing it gets stuck repeating the same search hundreds of times overnight. Which controls should the harness add?
o: A larger context window, so the agent can remember more of what it has already done
Step, time and cost budgets with loop detection, then stopping the run and escalating
Permission to delete old reports, so the shared drive doesn’t fill up during long runs
A second agent that watches the first and restarts it whenever it seems to be stuck
exam.why: Budgets and loop detection bound runaway behaviour, and escalation brings in a person. Bigger contexts don’t prevent loops, extra permissions raise risk, and automatic restarts can repeat the loop.

exam.q: A team updates the system prompt of a production RAG assistant to improve its tone. What is the BEST way to confirm the change is safe to release?
o: Check that the new prompt reads well and has been approved by the product owner
Run the regression, groundedness and guardrail test suites against the new prompt
Release it to all users and monitor the number of complaints over the next week
Compare the new prompt’s length with the old one, to confirm nothing was removed
exam.why: Prompt changes alter behaviour like code changes, so they need the same regression, groundedness and security behaviour tests with agreed thresholds. Approval of wording, complaint monitoring and length checks don’t show safety.

exam.q: During a failure test, the moderation API used to screen a chatbot’s replies times out. Logs show the chatbot sent replies to users without moderation while the API was down. What is the correct finding?
o: The test passed, because the chatbot stayed available throughout the outage
A defect: moderation must fail closed, holding or routing replies until it recovers
A minor issue, because most of the replies would probably have passed moderation anyway
The moderation API should be removed, because it reduces availability
exam.why: Security and safety checks must fail closed. Releasing unchecked content during an outage defeats the control; availability without the check isn’t a pass.

exam.q: An agent that books travel fails halfway through a task: the flight is booked but the hotel booking errors. On retry, it books a second flight. Which design changes BEST address this?
o: Increase the agent’s retry limit, so that it keeps trying until the hotel succeeds
Make bookings idempotent and track task state, so retries resume and partial work is handled
Remove the agent’s ability to book hotels, so that the task can no longer fail halfway
Ask users to check their bank statements for duplicate payments after each trip
exam.why: Idempotent actions and tracked state mean retries continue from where the task stopped instead of repeating completed steps, and partial work can be compensated or flagged. More retries make duplication worse, and the other options avoid the problem rather than fixing it.
